contexts.label: Education & learning
contexts.question: What must learners and teaching staff understand or be able to do, and who might be left out?

contexts.label: Workplace & business
contexts.question: How would this change work, skills, accountability and cost in a real organisation?

contexts.label: Community & public life
contexts.question: Whose voice or local knowledge should shape deployment, access and consent?

contexts.label: Environment & place
contexts.question: What energy, materials, infrastructure and ecological effects may be hidden by the headline?

technologies.title: Generative AI
technologies.teaser: Systems that generate text, images, audio or code from learned patterns.
technologies.scenario: A team wants to introduce a generative AI assistant into everyday work.

cards.text: Drafts text and summarises material from prompts.
cards.why: Generating content is a capability, although output quality varies.

cards.text: Can produce plausible but false statements.
cards.why: Confident errors are a limitation that calls for verification.

cards.text: Relies on model weights and computing infrastructure.
cards.why: Models require execution hardware and a deployed software system.

cards.text: Workers may gain speed but face changes in tasks and expectations.
cards.why: The workforce experiences both potential benefits and organisational impacts.

cards.text: Requires appropriate access to input data and documents.
cards.why: The usefulness and risks depend on which information the model can access.

cards.text: May assist with translation and idea generation.
cards.why: Supporting drafting and language tasks is a possible function.

cards.text: Sensitive prompts could disclose private information.
cards.why: Data privacy is a constraint on safe deployment.

cards.text: Needs evaluation and human checking in consequential uses.
cards.why: Oversight and testing are operational requirements for dependable use.

cards.text: Clients or learners may receive more accessible explanations.
cards.why: The people receiving AI-supported work can be affected.

cards.text: Can adapt the style of a response for a target audience.
cards.why: Prompt-based tailoring is a capability.

cards.text: Depends on network connectivity for cloud-hosted models.
cards.why: Cloud services need connectivity, although some models can run locally.

cards.text: May inherit patterns or biases present in training data.
cards.why: Unequal or biased outputs are a quality and fairness limitation.

blindspots.title: Accountability and escalation
blindspots.explanation: Someone must own mistakes, exceptions and decisions when the model is wrong.
blindspots.question: Who can intervene or override the model?

blindspots.title: Data governance
blindspots.explanation: Retention, consent, permitted use and access rules matter as much as the model itself.
blindspots.question: Can you explain where prompts and outputs go?

blindspots.title: Ongoing maintenance
blindspots.explanation: Models, policies, costs and user practices change after launch.
blindspots.question: How will you detect performance drift or misuse?

technologies.title: Digital Twins
technologies.teaser: A continuously informed digital representation of a physical system or process.
technologies.scenario: A city is considering a digital twin to improve how it manages infrastructure.

cards.text: Simulates what-if changes before trying them physically.
cards.why: Scenario testing is a central potential use of a digital twin.

cards.text: Requires reliable information about the real system.
cards.why: A twin is only as useful as the quality of its model and data.

cards.text: Outdated sensors can create a misleading picture.
cards.why: Poor data can make the representation inaccurate.

cards.text: Infrastructure operators can use it to plan maintenance.
cards.why: Operators are a primary stakeholder group.

cards.text: Needs a way to refresh data as conditions change.
cards.why: A living twin needs suitable data collection and integration.

cards.text: Can visualise assets, flows and system behaviour.
cards.why: Making complex system states visible is a capability.

cards.text: Building and validating detailed models takes resources.
cards.why: Model fidelity, cost and effort constrain adoption.

cards.text: Residents may be affected by decisions informed by it.
cards.why: People outside the technical team can experience downstream consequences.

cards.text: Depends on clearly defined model boundaries.
cards.why: A twin must specify what is represented and what is not.

cards.text: Can flag possible asset failures from patterns in data.
cards.why: Analysis can help anticipate problems where data and models support it.

cards.text: Requires people who can interpret and challenge outputs.
cards.why: Expertise is needed to use the model responsibly.

cards.text: Cannot represent every unexpected real-world event.
cards.why: Models are simplifications, not perfect copies of reality.

blindspots.title: Model ownership
blindspots.explanation: Maintenance responsibility and update processes are essential after the first demonstration.
blindspots.question: Who keeps the twin accurate next year?

blindspots.title: Interoperability
blindspots.explanation: Data often spans vendors, formats and departments that do not communicate cleanly.
blindspots.question: Which data systems must connect?

blindspots.title: Decision pathways
blindspots.explanation: A useful simulation does not automatically lead to better action.
blindspots.question: Who decides what to do with model outputs?

technologies.title: Augmented Reality
technologies.teaser: Digital information layered into a person’s view of the physical world.
technologies.scenario: An organisation wants to use augmented reality for workplace learning.

cards.text: Places visual instructions over a real task.
cards.why: Overlaying guidance is a common AR function.

cards.text: Needs suitable screens, cameras or wearable hardware.
cards.why: An interface must display digital content in the user’s environment.

cards.text: Eye strain or discomfort can interrupt use.
cards.why: Ergonomics affects how long and how safely people can use it.

cards.text: Learners may get contextual guidance at the point of work.
cards.why: The people being trained are directly affected.

cards.text: Requires a way to track position and surfaces.
cards.why: Registration and tracking help digital objects line up with the world.

cards.text: Can show a 3D model at real-world scale.
cards.why: Spatial placement is an AR capability.

cards.text: Occlusion and poor tracking can cause misalignment.
cards.why: Inaccurate overlays can reduce usability or trust.

cards.text: Bystanders can be affected by cameras in shared spaces.
cards.why: Camera-based interaction raises concerns beyond the primary user.

cards.text: Needs content designed for the specific task and environment.
cards.why: Context-sensitive content is essential for meaningful use.

cards.text: Can reveal hidden components of equipment visually.
cards.why: AR can illustrate information not directly visible.

cards.text: Depends on device power and battery life.
cards.why: Wearable or mobile systems need adequate power.

cards.text: Bright light, clutter or accessibility needs may limit usability.
cards.why: Environmental and human differences affect performance.

blindspots.title: Physical safety
blindspots.explanation: Users need to see hazards and stay attentive to their surroundings.
blindspots.question: Could an overlay hide a risk?

blindspots.title: Accessibility alternatives
blindspots.explanation: Not everyone can comfortably use headsets, gestures or visual cues.
blindspots.question: What equivalent non-AR pathway exists?

blindspots.title: Consent in shared spaces
blindspots.explanation: Bystanders may not expect a device to capture images of them.
blindspots.question: What is captured, stored or shared?

technologies.title: Edge AI
technologies.teaser: Running AI inference near where data is produced, rather than always in a distant cloud.
technologies.scenario: A manufacturer is exploring AI analysis on devices on the factory floor.

cards.text: Can analyse sensor data without sending every event to the cloud.
cards.why: Local inference is a central capability of edge AI.

cards.text: Needs hardware powerful enough for the chosen model.
cards.why: Processor, memory and acceleration limit which models can run.

cards.text: Small devices may struggle with large models.
cards.why: Compute, memory and energy budgets constrain performance.

cards.text: Maintenance teams may receive faster fault alerts.
cards.why: Operators and staff can be affected by predictions and alerts.

cards.text: Requires a model packaged for the target device.
cards.why: Deployment and optimisation must match hardware constraints.

cards.text: Can reduce latency for some real-time decisions.
cards.why: Processing nearby often shortens the network round trip.

cards.text: Different devices make updating software harder.
cards.why: Fleet management is an operational challenge.

cards.text: People being monitored may have privacy concerns.
cards.why: Sensor-based systems can affect workers or community members.

cards.text: Needs an approach for distributing secure updates.
cards.why: Devices must receive patches and model changes safely.

cards.text: Can continue some functions during a network outage.
cards.why: Local operation can reduce dependence on constant connectivity.

cards.text: Depends on sufficient sensor input quality.
cards.why: Poor observations cannot reliably support useful predictions.

cards.text: Offline operation does not guarantee privacy.
cards.why: Local devices can still log, share or leak personal data.

blindspots.title: Device lifecycle
blindspots.explanation: A deployed device needs support long after its first software release.
blindspots.question: How will older devices be patched?

blindspots.title: Physical security
blindspots.explanation: Hardware in public or distributed locations can be stolen or tampered with.
blindspots.question: What happens if someone accesses the device?

blindspots.title: Fallbacks
blindspots.explanation: Local automated decisions still need safe behaviour when sensors or models fail.
blindspots.question: What is the safe default when confidence is low?

technologies.title: Autonomous Delivery Robots
technologies.teaser: Mobile robots that move items through mapped or partially understood environments.
technologies.scenario: A campus is considering robots to deliver supplies between buildings.

cards.text: Can move small loads with limited direct supervision.
cards.why: Transporting goods is the robot’s intended service.

cards.text: Needs localisation, mapping and obstacle detection.
cards.why: Navigation requires sensing where the robot is and what is nearby.

cards.text: Uneven paths, stairs and weather limit reliable routes.
cards.why: Physical environments impose practical constraints.

cards.text: Pedestrians and people using mobility aids share the space.
cards.why: Public users of paths can be affected, whether or not they use the service.

cards.text: Requires reliable charging and maintenance arrangements.
cards.why: Power and upkeep support day-to-day operation.

cards.text: Can follow a route and adjust around obstacles.
cards.why: Path planning and avoidance are capabilities.

cards.text: Some edge cases still require remote human help.
cards.why: Real-world autonomy is bounded and can need intervention.

cards.text: Delivery workers and logistics teams may see tasks change.
cards.why: Automation changes job workflows.

cards.text: Needs appropriate permissions to operate in its area.
cards.why: Site rules and applicable law shape deployment.

cards.text: May provide predictable tracking and delivery updates.
cards.why: Status reporting can make logistics more visible.

cards.text: Depends on a reliable way to load and receive parcels.
cards.why: The whole service needs hand-off processes, not just motion.

cards.text: Vandalism or blocked routes can interrupt operation.
cards.why: Uncontrolled environments introduce disruption.

blindspots.title: Inclusive route design
blindspots.explanation: Routes must not block footpaths or create disproportionate accessibility barriers.
blindspots.question: Would the robot obstruct wheelchair users?

blindspots.title: Human override
blindspots.explanation: Staff need to recover stuck units and handle unusual incidents.
blindspots.question: Who responds when the robot stops?

blindspots.title: Service economics
blindspots.explanation: Purchase price is only one part of staffing, upkeep and replacement costs.
blindspots.question: What does a full year of operation cost?

technologies.title: Synthetic Biology
technologies.teaser: Engineering biological systems to perform useful functions.
technologies.scenario: A team is considering engineered microbes for a new material or manufacturing process.

cards.text: Can modify organisms to produce useful molecules.
cards.why: Engineering pathways for a desired output is a possible application.

cards.text: Requires a suitable biological host and design.
cards.why: The organism and engineered system must support the intended function.

cards.text: Biological performance may change outside lab conditions.
cards.why: Living systems can behave differently across environments.

cards.text: Communities may have concerns about environmental release.
cards.why: People in affected areas have legitimate stakes in decisions.

cards.text: Needs controlled testing and validated measurements.
cards.why: Evidence of performance and safety depends on good experiments.

cards.text: Can support new enzymes, materials or production methods.
cards.why: Biological manufacturing is a potential capability.

cards.text: Scaling from a lab to a factory can be difficult.
cards.why: Industrial conditions introduce yield and cost challenges.

cards.text: Workers may require new laboratory and safety skills.
cards.why: Operational roles and training requirements can change.

cards.text: Depends on appropriate biosafety controls and governance.
cards.why: Containment, oversight and rules are part of responsible use.

cards.text: Can make some production processes more targeted.
cards.why: Designed organisms can carry out specific transformations.

cards.text: Needs nutrients, equipment and reliable process conditions.
cards.why: Biological production depends on a stable operating environment.

cards.text: Unintended biological effects require evaluation.
cards.why: Complex biological interactions create uncertainty.

blindspots.title: Life-cycle impact
blindspots.explanation: A biological process is not automatically lower-impact once inputs and waste are counted.
blindspots.question: What energy, feedstocks and disposal routes are involved?

blindspots.title: Community engagement
blindspots.explanation: A project can affect groups whose views differ from the technical team’s.
blindspots.question: Who should shape the project before trials?

blindspots.title: Containment and recovery
blindspots.explanation: Responsible deployment must account for unexpected escape or process failure.
blindspots.question: What happens if containment fails?

technologies.title: Quantum Computing
technologies.teaser: Computing systems that manipulate quantum information rather than only classical bits.
technologies.scenario: An organisation is evaluating whether quantum computing could help with complex problems.

cards.text: May accelerate certain specialised algorithms.
cards.why: Quantum advantage is problem- and method-dependent, not universal.

cards.text: Needs high-quality qubits and precise control systems.
cards.why: Useful computation depends on quantum hardware and control.

cards.text: Qubits are susceptible to noise and errors.
cards.why: Noise is a major barrier to reliable long calculations.

cards.text: Researchers and specialised technical teams may benefit first.
cards.why: Early adoption tends to involve organisations with relevant expertise.

cards.text: Requires suitable algorithms for the target problem.
cards.why: A quantum device is not automatically useful for every workload.

cards.text: Can explore quantum systems through simulation techniques.
cards.why: Modelling quantum behaviour is an important potential use case.

cards.text: Fault-tolerant, large-scale capabilities remain difficult.
cards.why: Present systems have limitations and should not be oversold.

cards.text: Cybersecurity teams must plan for future cryptographic risks.
cards.why: Long-term cryptographic transition planning affects institutions.

cards.text: Needs error-management and calibration strategies.
cards.why: Maintaining useful calculations requires active error mitigation or correction.

cards.text: Uses superposition and entanglement as computational resources.
cards.why: These quantum properties underpin classes of algorithms.

cards.text: Some hardware designs require extreme cooling or vacuum systems.
cards.why: Physical requirements vary by qubit technology.

cards.text: Does not simply make all conventional computers obsolete.
cards.why: Quantum devices are specialised tools, not general-purpose replacements.

blindspots.title: Benchmark fairness
blindspots.explanation: Quantum claims should be compared against strong classical baselines.
blindspots.question: Which classical method was the benchmark?

blindspots.title: Hybrid workflows
blindspots.explanation: Quantum and classical computing often need to work together.
blindspots.question: Where does the quantum step sit in the full task?

blindspots.title: Skills and access
blindspots.explanation: Access to devices and people who understand them can be a major bottleneck.
blindspots.question: Who can validate and use the result?

technologies.title: Green Hydrogen
technologies.teaser: Hydrogen produced through electrolysis powered by low-emissions electricity.
technologies.scenario: A region is exploring green hydrogen for industrial use or transport.

cards.text: Can provide a fuel or feedstock for selected applications.
cards.why: Hydrogen can supply chemical and energy services.

cards.text: Needs electricity and water to run electrolysers.
cards.why: Electrolysis splits water using electrical energy.

cards.text: Energy losses occur in production, storage and use.
cards.why: Conversion steps reduce the efficiency of the full pathway.

cards.text: Industrial workers and nearby communities may be affected.
cards.why: New facilities change local jobs and infrastructure.

cards.text: Requires suitable storage and transport infrastructure.
cards.why: Hydrogen handling needs purpose-built systems and controls.

cards.text: Could replace some fossil-derived hydrogen in industry.
cards.why: Substitution in existing industrial demand is a credible use.

cards.text: High costs can limit commercial competitiveness.
cards.why: Costs depend on electricity, equipment and utilisation.

cards.text: Electricity users may compete for low-emissions power.
cards.why: Energy allocation can have broader system consequences.

cards.text: Needs safety procedures for a highly flammable gas.
cards.why: Safe storage, ventilation and leak detection are crucial.

cards.text: Can store energy for later conversion, with losses.
cards.why: Energy storage is possible but not always the most efficient use.

cards.text: Depends on credible assessment of electricity emissions.
cards.why: Environmental claims depend on how the power is generated.

cards.text: Is unlikely to be the best option for every energy need.
cards.why: Direct electrification may be more efficient in many cases.

blindspots.title: Opportunity cost of power
blindspots.explanation: Limited clean electricity could instead directly decarbonise other activities.
blindspots.question: What use of the electricity gives the best outcome?

blindspots.title: Water and place
blindspots.explanation: Water sourcing and local ecology need assessment in context.
blindspots.question: Who else relies on this water source?

blindspots.title: End-to-end carbon accounting
blindspots.explanation: Production labels alone may hide transport, leakage and energy-system emissions.
blindspots.question: Where are the system boundaries for the carbon claim?

technologies.title: 3D Bioprinting
technologies.teaser: Layer-by-layer deposition of cells and biomaterials to form tissue-like structures.
technologies.scenario: A research group is exploring printed tissue models for drug development.

cards.text: Can create structured tissue models for laboratory research.
cards.why: Producing tissue-like models is a current research application.

cards.text: Needs suitable cells, biomaterials and printing equipment.
cards.why: Living structures depend on viable biological inputs and tools.

cards.text: Keeping thick tissues alive can be difficult.
cards.why: Nutrient delivery and vascularisation remain major challenges.

cards.text: Researchers may use models to study disease or drug effects.
cards.why: Research teams and, indirectly, patients are stakeholders.

cards.text: Requires sterile processes and careful environmental control.
cards.why: Cell survival and contamination control depend on conditions.

cards.text: Can control where different materials and cells are deposited.
cards.why: Spatial placement is a defining technique.

cards.text: Printed structures may not behave like real organs.
cards.why: Biological fidelity and function are not guaranteed.

cards.text: Patients may be affected by future clinical claims and choices.
cards.why: The claims and expectations around research affect the public.

cards.text: Needs testing of cell viability and tissue function.
cards.why: Printed appearance alone does not demonstrate biological usefulness.

cards.text: May reduce reliance on some animal models in specific research.
cards.why: Better laboratory models could replace some experiments, case by case.

cards.text: Depends on design files and reproducible print settings.
cards.why: Repeatability requires controlled instructions and parameters.

cards.text: Printing transplant-ready organs is not a routine clinical service.
cards.why: The leap from models to fully functional transplant organs is substantial.

blindspots.title: Clinical translation
blindspots.explanation: Regulatory evidence and long-term safety would be required before medical use.
blindspots.question: What would need proving before use with a patient?

blindspots.title: Ethical cell sourcing
blindspots.explanation: Consent and provenance of biological samples matter.
blindspots.question: Where did the cells come from and with what permission?

blindspots.title: Reproducibility
blindspots.explanation: Small variations can change biological results between laboratories.
blindspots.question: Can another team reproduce the tissue properties?

technologies.title: Smart Grids
technologies.teaser: Electricity networks using digital sensing and control to manage changing supply and demand.
technologies.scenario: A council is considering smart-grid upgrades for a growing community.

cards.text: Can improve visibility of electricity demand and network conditions.
cards.why: Network sensing and analysis help operators observe change.

cards.text: Needs connected meters, sensors and control equipment.
cards.why: Digital monitoring requires instrumentation.

cards.text: Cyberattacks or network outages can disrupt operations.
cards.why: Connectivity adds new failure and security considerations.

cards.text: Households may get new ways to understand energy use.
cards.why: Customers can be affected by smart meters or pricing signals.

cards.text: Requires reliable communication between network components.
cards.why: Data and control signals must reach the right systems.

cards.text: Can help coordinate distributed solar and batteries.
cards.why: Managing two-way flows is an important capability.

cards.text: Legacy equipment can be expensive to integrate.
cards.why: Old infrastructure may not support modern digital interfaces.

cards.text: Electricity network operators may change working practices.
cards.why: Operating teams need new tools, skills and decisions.

cards.text: Needs clear safety rules and fallback operation.
cards.why: Grid reliability depends on safe behaviour during errors.

cards.text: May shift flexible consumption away from peak periods.
cards.why: Demand response can help manage peaks when appropriately designed.

cards.text: Depends on good data handling and access controls.
cards.why: Fine-grained use data deserves appropriate protection.

cards.text: Benefits may be uneven for people without flexible appliances.
cards.why: Not every customer can respond to pricing or automation.

blindspots.title: Equity in incentives
blindspots.explanation: Price schemes may disadvantage those unable to shift their energy demand.
blindspots.question: Who can and cannot benefit from the programme?

blindspots.title: Operational fallback
blindspots.explanation: Manual procedures must still work if digital coordination fails.
blindspots.question: What happens when communication is lost?

blindspots.title: Community trust
blindspots.explanation: Smart-meter data may reveal routines and raise concerns.
blindspots.question: How are consumers informed and involved?

technologies.title: Satellite Internet
technologies.teaser: Connectivity delivered through satellites and user terminals, including low-Earth-orbit systems.
technologies.scenario: A remote community is weighing satellite internet as an option for connectivity.

cards.text: Can deliver broadband to some areas without terrestrial fibre.
cards.why: Satellites can extend access where fixed networks are hard to reach.

cards.text: Needs a compatible user terminal and suitable sky view.
cards.why: Users need ground equipment with an appropriate link.

cards.text: Weather, obstacles or congestion can affect the service.
cards.why: Coverage and performance vary by environment and capacity.

cards.text: Rural residents may gain new remote-learning opportunities.
cards.why: People with limited existing internet are key stakeholders.

cards.text: Requires a functioning satellite constellation or network.
cards.why: The service depends on orbital infrastructure.

cards.text: Can support communication after some terrestrial failures.
cards.why: Alternative paths can aid resilience in some disasters.

cards.text: Affordability and power needs may block access.
cards.why: Equipment, subscriptions and energy cost money.

cards.text: Astronomers can be affected by the growing number of satellites.
cards.why: Night-sky observation and the space environment are affected.

cards.text: Needs ground gateways and wider internet connections.
cards.why: Satellites must connect users to broader networks.

cards.text: Enables mobile connectivity in suitable circumstances.
cards.why: Some services support moving vehicles or remote sites.

cards.text: Depends on spectrum allocation and regulatory permissions.
cards.why: Radio operation and coverage are subject to applicable rules.

cards.text: Space debris and network congestion create external costs.
cards.why: Scaling large constellations brings orbital and radio challenges.

blindspots.title: Local support
blindspots.explanation: Equipment failures are harder to resolve where technicians are far away.
blindspots.question: Who can maintain the terminal locally?

blindspots.title: Resilience assumptions
blindspots.explanation: An outage in power or ground infrastructure can interrupt satellite access too.
blindspots.question: Which dependencies remain during an emergency?

blindspots.title: Cultural and community fit
blindspots.explanation: Service design and governance should reflect how people actually use connectivity.
blindspots.question: Who gets to define successful access?

technologies.title: Decentralised Identity
technologies.teaser: Approaches to digital credentials in which people or organisations can present verifiable claims.
technologies.scenario: A training provider is considering portable digital credentials for learner achievements.

cards.text: Can let someone present a verifiable digital credential.
cards.why: Proof of a claim is a central purpose of credential systems.

cards.text: Needs trusted issuers and verification methods.
cards.why: Recipients must be able to check who issued a claim.

cards.text: Lost keys or credentials can make access difficult.
cards.why: Recovery and usability are major implementation challenges.

cards.text: Learners may gain greater portability for qualifications.
cards.why: Credential holders experience the service directly.

cards.text: Requires standards and interoperable data formats.
cards.why: Different wallets and systems must understand one another.

cards.text: Can support selective disclosure in some designs.
cards.why: Some credential protocols disclose only what is necessary.

cards.text: A cryptographic proof does not guarantee a claim is true.
cards.why: Issuers can be mistaken or dishonest despite valid signatures.

cards.text: Employers may need new verification processes.
cards.why: Organisations accepting credentials must adapt.

cards.text: Needs an accessible storage and recovery experience.
cards.why: People need to retain and regain control of their credentials.

cards.text: Can reduce repeated manual checks of some documents.
cards.why: Digital verification can simplify workflows.

cards.text: Depends on privacy-conscious revocation mechanisms.
cards.why: Expired or revoked credentials must be handled appropriately.

cards.text: Some people may lack suitable devices or digital skills.
cards.why: Digital-only systems can widen access gaps.

blindspots.title: Governance of trust
blindspots.explanation: Technical verification cannot replace decisions about whose authority is legitimate.
blindspots.question: Who decides which issuers are recognised?

blindspots.title: Consent and tracking
blindspots.explanation: Even valid credentials can be used to profile people across services.
blindspots.question: Can presentation be linked across organisations?

blindspots.title: Non-digital alternatives
blindspots.explanation: A portable wallet should not become the only way to prove eligibility.
blindspots.question: How does someone participate without a smartphone?
